title: Converting a DDA or L&DO Leasehold Flat in Delhi to Freehold: Where the Process Stands
meta_description: How DDA and L&DO leasehold flats in Delhi convert to freehold, what mutation involves, and the current freeze on fresh applications.
intro: Most flats and plots allotted by the Delhi Development Authority, and a good deal of the older housing stock in central Delhi that the Land and Development Office administers, were never sold outright. They were put on lease, with the allottee holding a leasehold interest rather than absolute ownership, and that lease carries conditions on use, construction and transfer that stay attached to the property no matter how many times it changes hands. Converting that leasehold interest to freehold is a distinct administrative step, separate from the original allotment and separate from any later sale, and it is the step most owners only think about when a buyer's lawyer asks for it or a bank wants clean title before sanctioning a loan.

This guide sets out how the DDA's conversion scheme actually works, why mutation turns out to be the real sticking point for many applicants, and why anyone relying on 'freehold' status for a DDA or L&DO property right now needs to check the current position carefully rather than assume the usual process is running. As of November 2026, it is not running in the ordinary way, and that fact changes what a seller, buyer or lender should expect in the near term.

sections.heading: Why the lease, not the sale deed, decides what you actually own
paragraphs: A flat allotted by the DDA is held under a lease deed executed between the allottee and the Authority, governed by the Delhi Development Act, 1957 and the scheme under which the particular flat was built. The lease deed, not any later agreement to sell, is the document that fixes the term, the ground rent if any, and the conditions on construction and use that bind the property. Every subsequent transferee steps into the same leasehold interest, subject to the same conditions, unless and until the Authority formally converts that interest into a freehold one.

The Land and Development Office works on a parallel but separate track. It administers a large stock of leasehold land in parts of central and south Delhi, much of it originally granted under the old Nazul land arrangement, and its own conversion process runs through a different office with its own forms and charges. A property owner should first establish which authority, DDA or L&DO, actually holds the lease before applying anywhere, because applying to the wrong office wastes months without moving the file forward.

sections.heading: What the conversion scheme actually involves
paragraphs: DDA's conversion scheme, set out in its own brochure for flats allotted by the Authority, lets an eligible leaseholder apply to have the leasehold interest converted into a freehold one on payment of a one-time conversion charge. That charge is calculated against the applicable rate schedule the DDA notifies from time to time, which has in recent years been pegged to the Delhi government's circle rates rather than a fixed figure, so the amount payable on any given flat has to be worked out at the time of application rather than assumed from an older transaction.

The brochure allows the conversion charge to be paid as a lump sum or spread over equal annual instalments across a period not exceeding five years, with interest applying to the deferred portion. Once the charge is paid and the file is cleared, the DDA issues a conveyance deed in place of the earlier lease deed, and that conveyance deed, once registered, is what actually changes the nature of the holding from leasehold to freehold. Paying the charge without getting the conveyance deed executed and registered does not, by itself, convert the title.

sections.heading: Mutation is usually the real obstacle, not the fee
paragraphs: Owners who have been through this process consistently report that the money is rarely the hold-up. The brochure itself makes conversion conditional on there being no pending dispute over who the current lessee actually is, and where an earlier transfer or inheritance has not been formally substituted in the DDA's own records, the conversion application sits until that mutation or substitution is completed first. In practical terms, this means a flat that passed through inheritance, a family settlement, or an unregistered transfer years ago can be blocked from freehold conversion today purely because nobody updated the DDA's lessee record at the time.

Recent Delhi High Court matters bear this out. In one 2025 case, the DDA resisted granting conversion on two separate grounds, the absence of a formal mutation application and non-deposit of what it called misuse charges, rather than on any dispute about the conversion fee itself. In another, the Court directed the DDA to complete conversion within a fixed period measured from the date mutation was granted, treating mutation as the gating event the whole conversion depended on. Anyone applying for conversion should assume mutation will be scrutinised and get that record straightened out before filing, rather than after the application is rejected for it.

sections.heading: Where the process stands as of late 2026
paragraphs: Fresh applications are not currently being accepted. Multiple reports place the suspension of DDA's online conversion portal in the first two months of 2026, with the Authority citing an internal review of the conversion policy and the charges attached to it; the precise date the portal went down is reported variously as early January or February, and the discrepancy itself is a sign that the position has not been formally and clearly communicated. A Union minister has stated publicly that the government intends to restore and simplify the conversion process, but no revised, notified policy had been confirmed as of this writing.

The Delhi High Court has been pressing the DDA on this directly. In DDA v. Mala Sahni Seth, the Court directed that pending applications be processed according to the policy that was in force on the date each application was filed, rather than leave applicants waiting indefinitely for a new policy, and asked the Authority to place any revised policy before it by the next hearing, now listed for 11 December 2026. Reports put the backlog of pending applications in the low thousands. The position at L&DO is less settled still, with one report suggesting conversions there had resumed using updated circle rates while other reporting describes the Office being pressed by the Court over continuing delays, so the two sources do not agree and the current status needs to be confirmed directly with the office handling the specific property rather than taken from either report alone.

sections.heading: What can stop a conversion even once the freeze lifts
paragraphs: Unauthorised construction on the property is one of the more common reasons a conversion application stalls once it is otherwise in order. Where the built structure departs from what the original allotment or sanctioned plan permitted, the Authority typically will not process conversion until the deviation is either regularised, where that is possible, or removed. A seller who has added an extra room or enclosed a balcony without sanction should expect this to surface during conversion, not just during a buyer's own due diligence.

Disputes between co-owners or within a family over who the rightful leaseholder is will also stop the file, since the Authority is not in a position to decide title disputes and will simply wait for the parties to resolve the question themselves, through a civil court if necessary, before it will record a mutation or process a conversion in anyone's name.

sections.heading: After conversion: registration and municipal mutation still have to follow
paragraphs: Getting the DDA's conveyance deed is not the end of the paperwork. The deed has to be registered with the sub-registrar under the Registration Act, 1908, with stamp duty paid under the Indian Stamp Act as applicable in Delhi, before it has full legal effect as a transfer of title. Only after registration should the owner apply to the Municipal Corporation of Delhi to have the property's tax and ownership records mutated to reflect the freehold status and the registered owner's name, since the DDA's own conversion file and the MCD's property tax register are maintained separately and one does not automatically update the other.

A buyer told that a flat is 'already freehold' should ask to see the registered conveyance deed itself, not just a letter from the DDA confirming conversion has been approved, and should separately check the MCD mutation record before closing. Relying on a seller's description of the status, without seeing both documents, is one of the more avoidable mistakes in these transactions.

sections.heading: What to do if you are mid-process or thinking of applying
paragraphs: If an application was filed before the portal was suspended, the Mala Sahni Seth direction means it should still be processed under the policy that applied on the filing date, and a prolonged silence from the Authority on an application that predates the freeze is something that can be pursued, including by writ if necessary, rather than simply waited out. If no application has yet been filed, it is worth using the pause to get the lessee record straightened out, confirming there is no pending mutation issue, misuse charge, or unregularised construction, so that whenever the window reopens the application itself does not face an avoidable rejection.

Given how often this position has shifted over the past year, and how differently L&DO and DDA each describe their own status, confirming the current rules with the specific office holding the lease, rather than relying on this guide or any single news report for the figure or the date, remains the safer course before committing to a transaction timeline.

faqs.q: Is DDA currently accepting new applications for leasehold-to-freehold conversion?
faqs.a: As of late 2026, no. Multiple reports describe the DDA's online conversion portal as suspended since early 2026 pending a policy review, with no revised policy confirmed as notified. The position is being monitored by the Delhi High Court, with the matter next listed in December 2026.

faqs.q: What happens to a conversion application filed before the freeze?
faqs.a: The Delhi High Court has directed that pending applications be processed under the policy that was in force on the date each application was filed, rather than left waiting for a new policy. A long delay on an application filed before the freeze can be pursued rather than treated as closed.

faqs.q: Why is my DDA flat's conversion stuck even though I am ready to pay the fee?
faqs.a: The fee is rarely the real obstacle. DDA's own conversion scheme makes conversion conditional on there being no pending mutation or substitution issue in its lessee records, and recent court matters show applications being resisted over exactly this, along with unpaid misuse charges, rather than over the conversion charge itself.

faqs.q: Does paying the conversion charge make my flat freehold?
faqs.a: No. Payment clears one condition, but the DDA still has to issue a conveyance deed, and that deed has to be registered under the Registration Act before the property's legal status actually changes from leasehold to freehold. A buyer should ask to see the registered deed, not just a payment receipt.

faqs.q: Is L&DO leasehold property converted the same way as a DDA flat?
faqs.a: The two run separate processes with separate forms and offices, since L&DO administers different leasehold land, much of it in central Delhi. Reports on L&DO's current status conflict with each other, so the position for a specific property should be confirmed directly with that office rather than assumed from the DDA position.

Registration Act, 1908 and the Indian Stamp Act as applicable in Delhi, on registration of the conveyance deed following conversion

verification_notes: DDA flats held on lease under the Delhi Development Act, 1957, with conversion a separate administrative step: confirmed from the DDA's own conversion brochure (dda.gov.in) and corroborated by secondary guides describing the same structure; a specific vesting section number was not independently double-confirmed, so no section number is cited for the Act itself.

Conversion charge payable lump sum or in instalments over up to five years, with interest on deferred payments: confirmed from the DDA's own brochure document and a separate news report describing the same instalment structure; the specific interest percentage reported in one source only was not used since it was not independently confirmed.

Mutation or substitution pending with the lessor blocking conversion, and 2025 Delhi High Court matters involving disputes over mutation and misuse charges: confirmed from the DDA brochure's own conditions and from independent reporting of two separate 2025 Delhi High Court rulings on this point.

Portal suspension in early 2026 pending policy review, and the DDA v. Mala Sahni Seth proceedings with a December 2026 listing: confirmed across multiple independent news reports and two separate verdictum.in case reports; the exact suspension date (reported as both January and February 2026) could not be reconciled between sources, so both are mentioned rather than one being stated as definite.

Conversion charge tied to circle rates rather than a fixed percentage for residential flats, and the 6-10% figures found in search results: the percentage figures found applied to commercial and industrial land in a dated proposal, not confirmed for residential flats from two sources, so no specific percentage is stated for residential conversion.

L&DO's current conversion status: two sources conflict (one describing resumption using updated circle rates, another describing continuing court-flagged delays), so the guide states the conflict rather than asserting either position as current.
